source.title: Polysemanticity or Polysemy? Lexical Identity Confounds Superposition Metrics

record.tranche_reason: The study provides new results arguing that lexical identity can inflate polysemanticity and SAE metrics, so observed overlap needs qualification before being attributed to superposition. It does not test the original toy-network mechanism.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own factorial overlap measurements, neuron analyses, SAE collision results, and lexical-subspace intervention. Results cited from prior work, including incidental polysemanticity, are not recorded as findings here. Downstream WSD and ROME performance results are omitted because they do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study's own factorial overlap measurements, neuron probes and ablations, and SAE collision analyses in nine trained transformers argue that measured polysemanticity is partly lexical identity rather than superposition. This bears directly on V3, and on V5 through the SAE features. It does not test the toy-model mechanism (V1) or capacity competition (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a substantial portion of what metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition. They say lexical signal must be separated before attributing remaining overlap to compression, and that genuine superposition is not denied.
record.recipe_differences: Measures factorial overlap and neuron/SAE properties in trained language models, rather than using the original toy-network setup or testing its feature-capacity mechanism.
record.method_sensitivity: The lexical contribution varies with layer depth and model architecture; bidirectional models show steeper declines with depth, while autoregressive models retain the ordering. The paper also reports differences by POS and dataset, although the PS > SYN ordering persists in the tested settings.
record.problems: The paper notes that absolute ablation effects are small. The primary overlap evidence is the condition ordering; some reported aggregates lack per-model numerical values in the main text. SAE collision figures are limited to tested SAEs and polysemous-word inputs, and the corrected score requires sense labels.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted WSD classifier and ROME editing outcomes (Section 5.9), which report downstream task/edit effects rather than directly measuring a claim version. Omitted additional synonym-subset, POS, and attention-representation analyses because the retained rows capture the principal lexical-overlap result and its replication.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no sparsity sweep or phase transition, no geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition, importance-based dedicated dimensions or feature sharing. The paper argues against capacity as the cause of the measured overlap but never manipulates capacity.
Only lexical identity in polysemous-word settings is tested as the alternative cause. Capacity pressure is not shown to be absent, and other causes are not tested.
Not tested whether features are distributed across neurons in general, or whether SAEs recover the model's true sparse features.
Stability across seeds or runs, completeness, and canonicity are not tested. Only sense blending in features active for polysemous words is measured.
Not tested whether features are one-dimensional or multi-dimensional. The lexical identity subspace is a confound subspace, not a test of feature dimensionality.

missing.what: The lexically adjusted polysemanticity score reclassifies only 6.5% (layer 6) to 10.4% (layer-averaged) of GPT-2 neurons flagged as polysemantic, with 93–94% of these confirmed as form detectors. This is the paper's most direct estimate of how much flagged polysemanticity is lexical, and it is smaller than the 'most shared neurons' framing.
Token-embedding baseline: Remb_lex is 0.71–0.89. MLP Rlex at layer 0 exceeds it in autoregressive models but not in BERT or ELECTRA.
Per-model Rlex by layer for BERT, ELECTRA, GPT-2-Medium, Pythia-12B and LLaMA-2-13B (minima 0.21–0.29). Same ordering holds in attention-head outputs and for Jaccard overlap.
missing.locator: Appendix B.1, Tables 4–5; Appendix E; Appendix C, Figure 6

record.verdict_notes: V3 support rests on treating same-word cross-sense activation as 'polysemanticity'. The authors themselves read sense-blind neurons as pre-disambiguation word-form encoding, which some would not count as polysemanticity in the toy-model sense. Their own corrected score reclassifies only about 10% of flagged neurons, so the magnitude of the confound is modest even though its existence is well supported. The SAE results concern features active for polysemous words only. No code release is stated, though the appendix says data is released with code.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-capacity sweep, sparse-feature representation test, or regular-geometry test.
Does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or sharing by less important features.
Tests lexical identity as an alternative explanation for measured overlap in polysemous-word settings; does not establish that capacity pressure is absent or test every other possible cause.
Does not test whether features are generally spread across many neurons or whether SAEs recover the model's underlying sparse features.
Tests whether SAE features can blend senses of polysemous words; does not test feature stability across runs or whether SAE features are canonical units in general.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Nine transformers (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared MLP-neuron overlap for same-word/different-sense (PS) and different-word/same-sense (SYN) sentence pairs.

conditions.value: nine transformers across four architecture families

rows.measure: Neuron-overlap cosine similarity, PS versus SYN
rows.note: The aggregate ordering is reported across all nine models; per-model numerical values are not given here.

source_check.problem: 407 is the full dataset size; SYN comparisons have coverage for only 251 words.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the lexical contribution ratio Rlex across layers.
rows.value: Rlex decreases from 0.74 to 0.29 across layers and remains above zero
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap confidence interval remains above zero at all layers; interval values not stated
rows.note: The result supports a persistent lexical contribution in this model, with magnitude varying by depth.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-70B
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-averaged overlap for PS and SYN conditions.
rows.note: The paper reports the same ordering at this scale.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Classified neurons using sense selectivity and measured sense accuracy from neuron-group activations.
rows.note: The paper describes the blind-neuron result as near chance.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Used neuron-group activations to classify word form.
rows.value: All groups perform comparably at approximately 85%
rows.note: The authors report that blind neurons encode word identity while performing poorly on sense classification.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Identified form detectors from word identity alone and classified them by sense selectivity.
rows.measure: Share of form detectors classified as sense-blind or sense-selective
rows.note: Sense labels were not used to identify the form detectors.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Mean-ablated sense-selective or sense-blind neurons and measured held-out sense accuracy.
rows.value: Ablating sense-selective neurons reduces accuracy by 8 percentage points; ablating sense-blind neurons reduces it by less than 1 percentage point
rows.uncertainty: The sense-blind change is described as indistinguishable from random variation
rows.note: The authors interpret the selective-neuron effect as causal necessity for sense-discriminating behavior and the blind-neuron effect as negligible.

source_check.correct: Clean sense accuracy averages 73%; selective-neuron ablation reduces it by 8 percentage points; blind-neuron ablation reduces it by less than 1 percentage point, indistinguishable from random variation.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3; Appendix D, sense accuracy after ablation
source_check.problem: The pack truncates the value and uncertainty; the source supplies the complete result.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured sense-blind SAE features among active features for polysemous words.
rows.measure: Share of active features that are sense-blind
rows.note: The paper says the 128k SAE, with four times the feature capacity, produces nearly identical ratios.
rows.check: This is an SAE-feature result: 18–32% of active features are sense-blind. It is used in the V5 label but was linked only to V3. Link it to V5. The share is a minority, so the state against V5 is partial.

rows.subject: GPT-2 SAE feature #5132 (32k SAE, layer 8)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected feature activations across polysemous words.
rows.measure: Sense discriminability and input firing density
rows.value: Cohen's d < 0.5 across the reported words; fires on 47.5% of all inputs
rows.note: The paper characterizes the feature as encoding lexical form rather than a coherent concept.
rows.check: A single SAE feature (#5132) firing sense-blind across 232 words bears on whether SAE features are concept-level units (V5), not on neuron polysemanticity (V3). It is an illustrative case, not a rate.

rows.subject: Models in the standard polysemanticity-score analysis
rows.operation_detail: Examined word-form identity among activating input pairs for neurons flagged by standard polysemanticity scores.
rows.measure: Share of activating input pairs that share a word form
rows.note: The authors caution this is not a global inflation rate.
rows.check: The subject is wrong: the text does not name the model. It is likely GPT-2, the primary model, but this is not stated. The ≈57% applies only to polysemous inputs, which the authors stress is not a global rate.

source_check.problem: The source does not explicitly identify the model for this analysis; 57% is conditional on polysemous inputs.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the effect of projecting out top components of a lexical identity subspace on the PS–SYN cosine gap.
rows.note: The reported reduction is part of the stated 37–51% decrease from removing 20 LIS dimensions across GPT-2 and Pythia-1B.
rows.check: The note says 37–51% applies to the gap, but Table 10's caption gives it as the Rlex reduction. The GPT-2 values are correct (gap 0.119→0.047; Rlex 0.65→0.41).

source_check.correct: GPT-2, k=20: PS–SYN gap 0.119→0.047; Rlex 0.65→0.41; 0.7% of dimensions removed. Table 10 attributes the cross-model 37–51% reduction to Rlex, not the gap.
source_check.problem: The main values are correct, but the note associates 37–51% with the wrong metric; Section 5.8 itself contains this inconsistency.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the PS–SYN gap after projecting out lexical identity subspace components.
rows.note: At this projection size the gap reverses; the authors describe the confound as eliminated.
rows.check: The state 'reversed' is wrong relative to V3. The PS–SYN gap turning negative after removing 50 lexical-subspace dimensions shows the excess overlap is carried by word-form directions, which is consistent with V3. The value is correct (−0.028; Rlex < 0).

rows.subject: GPT-2 SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Compared active and sense-blind SAE features for polysemous words across layers.
rows.measure: Collision ratio: sense-blind active features divided by active features
rows.note: The study reports similar collision ratios despite a fourfold difference in dictionary size; these results challenge the interpretation of all such features as sense-level canonical units but do not test stability.
rows.check: No fix needed. These are collision ratios across five layers for two dictionary sizes, and the ratios do not fall with the 4× larger dictionary.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M SAE features
rows.operation_detail: Measured the proportion of active SAE features that conflate senses of the same word.
rows.note: The result is reported as a range across layers; layer-specific values are not stated in the main text.
rows.check: No fix needed. Per-layer values are not given in the main text.

rows.subject: GPT-2, BERT-base, and Pythia-1B
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the four-condition decomposition using sense-annotated Wikipedia sentences.
rows.measure: PS versus SYN cosine similarity across layers
rows.value: PS > SYN in all three models; significance at every layer
rows.uncertainty: GPT-2 p < .001; BERT-base p < .01; Pythia-1B p < .001; Holm-Bonferroni corrected
rows.note: The full SL > PS > SYN > CL ordering holds at the majority of layers; SYN and CL converge at a few late layers.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix F.1, Table 11 and accompanying paragraphs
source_check.problem: The reported all-layer ordering conflicts with Table 11's final-layer means for BERT and Pythia; the row accurately reproduces the authors' explicit claim.

relationships.condition: MLP neurons of nine transformers (110M–70B) on SemCor polysemous words, plus Wikipedia validation on GPT-2, BERT and Pythia-1B
relationships.reason: Same-word/different-sense overlap exceeds different-word/same-sense overlap in all models (r1–r3, r15). Form detectors are mostly sense-blind and carry word identity but little sense information (r4–r6). Ablating them barely affects sense accuracy (r7). Removing a small lexical subspace closes the gap (r11, r12). About 57% of flagged input pairs share a word form (r10).
relationships.display_finding: In every model, neuron overlap was larger for the same word in different senses than for different words with the same sense, and form-detector neurons were mostly sense-blind, with ablating them barely changing sense accuracy. Removing a small lexical subspace closed the gap, and about 57% of flagged input pairs shared a word form.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: MLP neurons of nine transformers (110M–70B) on SemCor polysemous words, plus Wikipedia validation on GPT-2, BERT and Pythia-1B
source_check.reason: r1–r7, r10–r12 and r15 support V3's evidential caution: lexical identity explains apparent multi-sense activation. This does not establish polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.

relationships.condition: Pre-trained GPT-2 (32k/128k) and Pythia-410M (65k) SAE features active for tested polysemous words
relationships.reason: 18–36% of active features are sense-blind, i.e. word-form units rather than concept units. The ratio does not drop with a 4× larger dictionary (r8, r9, r13, r14). The majority of active features are not blended.
relationships.display_finding: 18–36% of active features were sense-blind word-form units rather than concept units, the ratio did not fall with a 4× larger dictionary, and most active features were not blended.

source_check.condition: Pre-trained GPT-2 (32k/128k) and Pythia-410M (65k) SAE features active for tested polysemous words
source_check.reason: Sense-blind lexical features and similar collision rates across dictionary sizes test semantic interpretation, not completeness, stability or canonicality. Word-form features can themselves be representational units; these results do not establish a tested failure of V5.

reader_labels.condition: Tested transformer MLP representations of polysemous words, including the modern Wikipedia validation
reader_labels.reason: Shared word form produces greater overlap than shared meaning, and sense-blind neurons/features encode word identity while carrying little measured sense information (r1–r10, r15).
